summaries.example: Imagine building a small wooden house. The wood is the material cause because it is what the house is made from. The shape and plan are related to its form. The carpenter is an efficient cause because the carpenter starts the building. The purpose of making a shelter is the final cause. Aristotle thinks a full explanation may need all four kinds of cause.
summaries.summary: Aristotle’s natural philosophy is his organized study of the natural world. He asks what nature is, how change happens, and what makes events understandable. He describes nature as an inner source of change and rest. He also says that one event can have several causes. Matter is what something is made of, form is its structure or kind, an efficient cause starts or produces a change, and a final cause is what the change is for. Aristotle explains motion as the becoming-real of a possibility. For example, materials that can become a house are gradually made into one. Change involves something that gains a form, something that lacks that form at first, and a subject that remains through the process. Aristotle also distinguishes natural changes from forced changes. He argues that every motion needs a mover and that the universe depends on eternal heavenly motion. Behind those motions, he argues for an unmoved mover. This is not an ordinary physical object; it belongs beyond the physical domain.
key_ideas: Aristotle studies nature by asking how things change, rest, and behave.
He says nature can help explain a thing’s ordinary changes and rests.
A complete explanation may use matter, form, an efficient cause, and a goal or purpose.
Motion is the becoming-real of a possibility, such as a seed growing into a plant.
Aristotle connects the motions of the world to eternal heavenly motions and an unmoved mover.
summaries.why_it_matters: Aristotle’s questions encourage us to look for more than one part of an explanation. We can ask what something is made of, what shape or organization it has, what produced it, and what it is meant to do. His ideas also show how philosophers try to connect small changes, such as growth or building, with a large picture of the whole universe.

important_terms.definition: An inner principle that helps explain why a natural thing changes or stays still in certain ways.
A responsible factor in an explanation. Aristotle groups causes into four kinds.
What something is made from, such as wood used to make a house.
The arrangement or kind of thing that makes something what it is, such as a house’s structure.
A change or process, such as becoming warmer, growing, or moving to another place.
The ability for something to happen or become possible before it is fully real.
A being Aristotle says explains the eternal motions of the heavens without itself being moved.

questions_to_think_about: When you explain how something was made, do you talk about its materials, shape, maker, and purpose?
Is a thing’s usual behavior enough to explain what it does?
Can something be changing while it is still not finished becoming what it will be?

summaries.example: Consider a craftsman making a wooden chair. The wood supplies the material cause, while the chair’s organization supplies its formal cause. The craftsman’s skill and activity are connected with the efficient cause, and the chair’s use as a seat supplies a final-cause explanation. Aristotle’s framework does not treat these as interchangeable: what explains the chair’s material properties differs from what explains its structure, production, or purpose. The example also shows why form and matter cooperate: suitable material is required for the form to be realized.
summaries.summary:
Aristotle’s natural philosophy supplies a general framework for explaining natural entities and their changes. Nature is an internal principle of change and rest. This distinguishes natural behavior from changes produced through the interaction of an external active potentiality with a passive potentiality, although Aristotle’s account contains important qualifications. Explanations use four causal roles. Matter and form are the components of a matter-form composite: matter supplies relevant possibilities, while form organizes and actualizes them. Efficient or moving causes initiate processes, and final causes explain what processes are for. A cause may be internal, and form and final cause can sometimes coincide.

Aristotle defines motion through potentiality and actuality. Motion is not simply a potentiality, a privation, or the finished state reached at the end. It is an incomplete actuality of a potential while that potential is being realized. A change involves a subject, a form acquired at the end, and an initial lack of that form. The active and passive potentialities involved in a change must correspond. Aristotle also develops a principle of causational synonymy: fundamentally, a cause has the relevant form in actuality and brings it about in something that has it potentially. He qualifies this principle for locomotion, second actualities, and causal chains in generation and production, while maintaining that the principle remains valid at the appropriate level of explanation.

key_ideas: Aristotle presents natural philosophy as a unified inquiry into nature, motion, causation, place, time, and natural entities.
Nature is an internal principle of change and rest, contrasted with external active and passive capacities in non-natural changes.
The four causes divide explanatory roles: material, formal, efficient, and final. Matter and form cooperate in a matter-form composite.
Motion is neither merely a potentiality, a lack, nor the completed result; it is an incomplete actuality of a potential insofar as it remains potential.
Active and passive potentialities must match in an interaction, while Aristotle’s principle of causational synonymy connects the actual form in a cause with the form produced.
Locomotion has priority because changing entities generally need contact, and contact ordinarily requires movement. Aristotle links eternal celestial motion to an unmoved mover.
summaries.why_it_matters: Aristotle’s framework shows how a theory of nature can join several kinds of explanation rather than reducing every event to one mechanism. His distinctions between potentiality and actuality, process and result, internal nature and external agency, and natural and forced motion influenced later philosophical discussions of change and causation. Studying the argument also teaches an important philosophical habit: examine a broad principle, then test how it must be qualified in different cases.

important_terms.definition: An internal source of change and rest belonging to a natural entity; it helps explain the entity’s characteristic behavior.
A responsible explanatory factor. Aristotle distinguishes material, formal, efficient or moving, and final causes.
The underlying material component of a thing in a matter-form analysis.
The organizing aspect that makes a thing the kind of thing it is and can be causally significant.
The realization of a potential, specifically the ongoing realization involved while a process is incomplete.
A capacity or possibility for a state or activity that is not yet fully realized.
The principle that, in the basic causal pattern, a cause transmits a form it possesses in actuality to what has it potentially.
A mover that is not itself moved and that Aristotle uses to explain the persistence of eternal celestial motion.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining what a thing is made of explain its behavior, or is an account of its form also needed?
How does Aristotle’s distinction between a process and its completed result avoid defining change simply as ‘the ability to change’?
Why might locomotion be basic for other changes if interaction requires contact?
Do the qualifications to causational synonymy weaken the principle, or show how Aristotle is refining it?
What is gained, and what remains unclear, by explaining celestial motion through an unmoved mover?

summaries.example: Suppose a skateboard rolls down a ramp after someone pushes it. The push is an efficient cause because it begins the motion. The board’s shape and structure are part of its form, and its material is its matter. The ramp and wheels help explain how the motion can happen. Aristotle would also ask whether the motion fits the thing’s nature or is forced by something outside it. This shows why he thinks one event may need several kinds of explanation.
summaries.summary:
Aristotle’s natural philosophy asks how the natural world is organized and how its changes can be explained. He begins with nature, which he describes as an internal source of change and rest. A natural thing behaves in ways connected with what it is. By contrast, changes that are not natural require an active power in one thing and a passive capacity in another. These capacities must fit: something able to heat must meet something able to be heated.

Aristotle’s theory of the four causes gives different ways of being responsible. Matter is what a thing is made from, and form is its organization or kind. An efficient, or moving, cause starts a process, while a final cause explains its aim or purpose. A house, for instance, needs suitable building materials, a house-shaped arrangement, a builder’s activity, and a reason for being built. Matter and form are not rival explanations; they work together, because suitable matter is needed for a form to be realized.

Aristotle defines motion using potentiality and actuality. A thing can have a possibility without yet having the finished feature. Motion is the incomplete realization of that possibility while the process is occurring. It involves a subject, a form gained at the end, and an initial absence of that form. Aristotle also argues that causes generally produce a form they possess in actuality, a view often called causational synonymy. He qualifies this idea in cases such as locomotion, activities that follow an already acquired condition, and long causal chains.

key_ideas: Aristotle treats the study of nature as a connected investigation of change, causes, and the behavior of natural things.
A nature is an inner source of change or rest, while some changes happen through active and passive powers working together.
His four causes answer different questions: what something is made of, what it is, what produces it, and what it is for.
Motion is the ongoing realization of a possibility, not simply the possibility or the finished result.
Aristotle says changes can be natural or forced, and he argues that every motion has a mover.
He gives locomotion a special place because contact for other interactions usually depends on things moving together.
summaries.why_it_matters: Aristotle’s account matters because it asks us to separate questions that are often mixed together. What is something made from? What kind of thing is it? What caused it? What is it for? His analysis also gives precise tools for thinking about change: a possibility, its realization, the subject that changes, and the mover involved. These distinctions help readers compare different explanations instead of assuming that every event has only one kind of cause.

important_terms.definition: An internal source that helps explain why a natural thing changes or remains at rest.
Something responsible for an event or feature. Aristotle identifies four main kinds of cause.
The material from which a thing is made.
The organization or structure that makes a thing the kind of thing it is.
A process of change, including change in substance, quality, amount, or place.
A possibility or ability that can become real.
The actual condition or activity that realizes a possibility.
A cause that is not itself moved and is proposed to explain eternal celestial motion.

questions_to_think_about: Can one event have several correct explanations at the same time?
What is the difference between something being able to change and actually changing?
Would a natural change still need a mover? How does Aristotle answer this for living things and elements?
Why does Aristotle give movement from place to place a special role?
What reasons does he give for thinking that eternal motions require an unmoved mover?
